claim: Drosophila melanogaster can suppress and reverse the optomotor turning response over several seconds under certain stimulus conditions.
source: Here, we report that under certain stimulus conditions, two Drosophila species, including the widely studied Drosophila melanogaster, can suppress and even reverse the optomotor turning response over several seconds.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by behavioral data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila yakuba can suppress and reverse the optomotor turning response over several seconds under certain stimulus conditions.
source: Here, we report that under certain stimulus conditions, two Drosophila species, including the widely studied Drosophila melanogaster, can suppress and even reverse the optomotor turning response over several seconds.
evidence: The abstract states this finding for two species, and Figure 1e shows data for D. yakuba.

claim: Anti-directional turning is most strongly evoked by long-lasting, high-contrast, slow-moving visual stimuli.
source: Such 'anti-directional turning' is most strongly evoked by long-lasting, high-contrast, slow-moving visual stimuli that are distinct from those that promote syn-directional optomotor turning.
evidence: The abstract states this, and it is supported by data in Figure 2 showing spatiotemporal tuning.

claim: Anti-directional turning requires the local motion detecting neurons T4 and T5.
source: Anti-directional turning, like the syn-directional optomotor response, requires the local motion detecting neurons T4 and T5.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4a shows that silencing T4 and T5 eliminates anti-directional turning.

claim: CH cells show involvement in anti-directional turning responses.
source: A subset of lobula plate tangential cells, CH cells, show involvement in these responses.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4c shows that silencing CH neurons reduces anti-directional turning.

claim: Direction-selective cells in the lobula plate show no evidence of dynamics that match the anti-directional turning behavior.
source: Imaging from a variety of direction-selective cells in the lobula plate shows no evidence of dynamics that match the behavior, suggesting that the observed inversion in turning direction emerges downstream of the lobula plate.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 5 shows calcium imaging data from T4, T5, HS, and CH neurons that do not show reversal dynamics.

claim: The inversion in turning direction emerges downstream of the lobula plate.
source: Imaging from a variety of direction-selective cells in the lobula plate shows no evidence of dynamics that match the behavior, suggesting that the observed inversion in turning direction emerges downstream of the lobula plate.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the imaging data showing no reversal in lobula plate neurons.

claim: Anti-directional turning declines with age.
source: Further, anti-directional turning declines with age and exposure to light.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 6 shows behavioral data across different ages.

claim: Anti-directional turning declines with exposure to light.
source: Further, anti-directional turning declines with age and exposure to light.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 6 shows that dark-reared flies maintain stronger anti-directional responses.

claim: Drosophila optomotor turning behaviors contain rich, stimulus-dependent dynamics that are inconsistent with simple reflexive stabilization responses.
source: These results show that Drosophila optomotor turning behaviors contain rich, stimulus-dependent dynamics that are inconsistent with simple reflexive stabilization responses.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the overall findings.

claim: The optomotor response is thought to be a course stabilizing mechanism that minimizes retinal slip.
source: In insects, this response is thought to be a course stabilizing mechanism that minimizes retinal slip, allowing animals to maintain their trajectory in the face of external or unexpected rotational forces (Götz and Wenking, 1973; Götz, 1975).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Photoreceptor signals are split into parallel ON and OFF pathways in the lamina and medulla.
source: Photoreceptor signals are split into parallel ON and OFF pathways in the lamina and medulla (Joesch et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2011; Behnia et al., 2014; Strother et al., 2014), which are not direction-selective.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: ON and OFF pathways in the lamina and medulla are not direction-selective.
source: Photoreceptor signals are split into parallel ON and OFF pathways in the lamina and medulla (Joesch et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2011; Behnia et al., 2014; Strother et al., 2014), which are not direction-selective.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: T4 and T5 cells compute direction-selective responses along four directions at every point in the fly visual field.
source: These signals provide input to T4 and T5 cells, which compute direction-selective responses along four directions at every point in the fly visual field (Bausenwein et al., 1992; Maisak et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2013; Shinomiya et al., 2019; Henning et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The outputs of T4 and T5 cells are summed across visual space by lobula plate tangential cells (LPTCs).
source: The outputs of T4 and T5 cells are then summed across visual space by lobula plate tangential cells (LPTCs) (Joesch et al., 2008; Schnell et al., 2012; Maisak et al., 2013; Mauss et al., 2015; Barnhart et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Different LPTCs provide distinct signals about the overall pattern of motion surrounding the fly.
source: Different LPTCs provide distinct signals about the overall pattern of motion surrounding the fly, and have been linked to head and body movements (Krapp and Hengstenberg, 1996; Haikala et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: LPTCs have been linked to head and body movements.
source: Different LPTCs provide distinct signals about the overall pattern of motion surrounding the fly, and have been linked to head and body movements (Krapp and Hengstenberg, 1996; Haikala et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Some counter-intuitive turning behaviors in flies can be accounted for by aliasing when using periodic stimuli with spatial wavelengths smaller than the receptive field of individual ommatidia.
source: In some cases, these counter-intuitive behaviors were observed using periodic stimuli with spatial wavelengths smaller than the receptive field of individual ommatidia, and thus can be accounted for by aliasing (Götz, 1964; Götz, 1970; Buchner, 1976).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for prior observations with citations.

claim: When a moving pattern is presented in front of a tethered flying fly, the animal turns in the direction of the stimulus motion.
source: Work in a tethered flight simulator showed that when a moving pattern is presented in front of the fly, the animal turned in the direction of the stimulus motion (Tammero et al., 2004), as expected (Götz, 1968).
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding with citations.

claim: When a moving pattern is presented behind a tethered flying fly, the animal attempts to turn in the direction opposite to stimulus motion.
source: However, if the moving pattern was presented behind the fly, it attempted to turn in the direction opposite to stimulus motion (Tammero et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding with citation.

claim: Freely walking flies presented with rotational patterns on a dome generally turn in the direction of motion, but these rotations are often punctuated by brief, large-magnitude saccades in the opposite direction.
source: In a different experimental preparation, rotational patterns were presented on a dome around freely walking flies (Williamson et al., 2018). Under these conditions, flies generally turned in the direction of motion of the stimulus, but these rotations were often punctuated by brief, large-magnitude saccades in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding with citation.

claim: Experiments using flight simulators have reported spikes in torque in the direction opposite the stimulus rotation.
source: Similarly, experiments using flight simulators have reported spikes in the torque in the direction opposite the stimulus rotation (Wolf and Heisenberg, 1990).
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding with citation.

claim: Zebrafish have been observed to turn in the opposite direction of optic flow under certain conditions.
source: Interestingly, zebrafish have also been observed to turn in the opposite direction of optic flow under certain conditions (Bak-Coleman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding with citation.

claim: Low-contrast, slow-moving sinusoidal gratings cause flies to turn in the same direction as the moving gratings via the classical optomotor turning response.
source: As expected, low-contrast, slow-moving sinusoidal gratings caused flies to turn in the same direction as the moving gratings via the classical optomotor turning response (Figure 1b; Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956; Götz, 1964; Buchner, 1976; Tammero et al., 2004; Seelig et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2011; Bahl et al., 2013; Silies et al., 2013; Clark et al., 2014; Bahl et al., 2015; Leonhardt et al., 2016; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016; Strother et al., 2017; Creamer et al., 2018; Strother et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: When presented with high-contrast sinusoidal gratings, flies turn in the stimulus direction for approximately 1 s, then reverse course and turn in the direction opposite to the stimulus motion for the duration of the stimulus presentation.
source: However, when we changed the stimulus to high-contrast sinusoidal gratings (nominal 100% Weber contrast), flies turned in the stimulus direction for approximately 1 s, but then reversed course, and turned in the direction opposite to the stimulus motion for the duration of the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: As contrast increases from 0 to 0.5, flies turn faster during the first 500 ms of stimulus presentation, reaching a plateau at around 0.5 contrast.
source: As contrast increased, the flies turned faster during the first half second of stimulus presentation, reaching a plateau at around 0.5 contrast, consistent with previous results (McCann and MacGinitie, 1965; Buchner, 1976; Heisenberg and Buchner, 1977; Duistermars et al., 2007; Bahl et al., 2015; Strother et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: At contrasts between 0 and 0.25, flies turn in the same direction as the stimulus after the first second of stimulation, with faster turning as the contrast increases.
source: At contrasts between 0 and 0.25, flies turned in the same direction as the stimulus, with faster turning as the contrast increased.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1c data.

claim: When contrast is greater than 0.25, sustained turning decreases, lowering to no net sustained turning at around 0.8 contrast.
source: When the contrast was greater than 0.25, turning decreased, lowering to no net sustained turning at around 0.8 contrast.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1c data.

claim: Above a contrast of 0.8, flies begin to turn in the direction opposite the stimulus.
source: Above a contrast of 0.8, flies began to turn in the direction opposite the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1c data.

claim: Canton-S D. melanogaster strain displays milder but significant anti-directional turning at long timescales.
source: Indeed, when we tested a Canton-S D. melanogaster strain, we observed milder but significant anti-directional turning at long timescales (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Anti-directional turning is strongly linked to display brightness.
source: In our experiments, anti-directional turning was strongly linked to display brightness (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: When mean brightness of screens is reduced from 100 cd/m2 to 1 cd/m2, there is no anti-directional turning in 5 s trials.
source: When the mean brightness of the screens was reduced from 100 cd/m2 to 1 cd/m2, we saw no anti-directional turning in 5 s trials (though average optomotor behavior did decrease over the course of the stimulus presentation).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1—figure supplement 2a data.

claim: When mean brightness is reduced to 0.1 cd/m2, flies persist in their optomotor behavior throughout the stimulus presentation.
source: When we further reduced the mean brightness to 0.1 cd/m2, flies persisted in their optomotor behavior throughout the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 1—figure supplement 2a data.

claim: Rearing D. melanogaster at 25°C instead of 20°C reduces overall turning behavior and eliminates anti-directional turning.
source: In particular, rearing D. melanogaster at 25°C instead of 20°C or testing flies that were 2 weeks old instead of 12–60 hr old both reduced overall turning behavior and eliminated anti-directional turning.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Testing flies that are 2 weeks old instead of 12–60 hr old reduces overall turning behavior and eliminates anti-directional turning.
source: In particular, rearing D. melanogaster at 25°C instead of 20°C or testing flies that were 2 weeks old instead of 12–60 hr old both reduced overall turning behavior and eliminated anti-directional turning.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: D. melanogaster always turn in the optomotor direction during the early stimulus response (first quarter second).
source: D. melanogaster always turned in the optomotor direction during the early stimulus response.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2a data.

claim: In the early response, flies turn most vigorously to stimuli with short spatial frequencies (~20° wavelength) and fast temporal frequencies (~8 Hz).
source: In this early response, flies turned most vigorously to stimuli with short spatial frequencies (~20° wavelength) and fast temporal frequencies (~8 Hz), in agreement with earlier studies (Tammero et al., 2004; Creamer et al., 2018; Strother et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: During the longer-timescale response to high-contrast stimuli, flies only turn in the optomotor direction at very high temporal frequencies (>~16 Hz) and at very low temporal frequencies (<0.5 Hz).
source: However, during the longer-timescale response to high-contrast stimuli, flies only turned in the optomotor direction at very high temporal frequencies (>~16 Hz) and at very low temporal frequencies (<0.5 Hz).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2b data.

claim: At intermediate temporal frequencies, flies show a sustained anti-directional response.
source: At intermediate temporal frequencies, flies showed a sustained anti-directional response.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2b data.

claim: The maximal anti-directional response is achieved at 1 Hz and 45° wavelength.
source: The maximal anti-directional response was achieved at 1 Hz and 45° wavelength, distinct from the conditions for peak classical turning responses.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2b data.

claim: The stimuli that elicit the strongest anti-directional response appear similar to those that maximally activate T4 and T5 neurons when measured in head-fixed flies.
source: Interestingly, the stimuli that elicit the strongest anti-directional response appear similar to those that maximally activate T4 and T5 neurons when those neurons are measured in head-fixed flies (Maisak et al., 2013; Leong et al., 2016; Arenz et al., 2017; Creamer et al., 2018; Strother et al., 2018; Wienecke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations to prior work.

claim: After switching from high contrast to low contrast, flies quickly revert to classical, syn-directional optomotor behavior.
source: After the switch to low contrast, the flies quickly reverted classical, syn-directional optomotor behavior, demonstrating that no long-term switch in directional turning occurs during high-contrast stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2c data.

claim: No long-term switch in directional turning occurs during high-contrast stimulus presentation.
source: After the switch to low contrast, the flies quickly reverted classical, syn-directional optomotor behavior, demonstrating that no long-term switch in directional turning occurs during high-contrast stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the contrast-switching experiment in Figure 2c.

claim: A rotating stimulus consisting of 5°-wide vertical bars with randomly chosen, binary contrasts yields similar behavioral responses to sinusoidal stimuli.
source: This effect did not depend on the periodic nature of these stimuli: a rotating stimulus consisting of 5°-wide vertical bars with randomly chosen, binary contrasts (Clark et al., 2014) yielded similar behavioral responses (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Adapting with front-to-back stimuli does not have a strong effect on the subsequent response to rotational stimuli.
source: We found that adapting with a stationary or closed-loop high-contrast sinusoid had little effect on the behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Similarly, adapting the fly with front-to-back stimuli did not have a strong effect on the subsequent response to rotational stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Adapting with back-to-front stimuli generates responses that no longer show an initial syn-directional turning response, but instead exhibit anti-directional turning immediately after the rotational stimulus begins.
source: However, adapting with back-to-front stimuli generated responses that no longer showed an initial syn-directional turning response, but instead exhibited anti-directional turning immediately after the rotational stimulus began.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2e data.

claim: Anti-directional turning results from slow-timescale changes that depend on strong back-to-front motion.
source: This result indicates that the anti-directional turning results from slow-timescale changes that depend on strong back-to-front motion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the adaptation experiments.

claim: Flies display anti-directional turning when presented with stimuli only in the front region (90° in front of the fly).
source: We found that flies displayed anti-directional turning when presented with stimuli only in the front region or only just in front of the midline (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3b, c.

claim: Flies display anti-directional turning when presented with stimuli only just in front of the midline (45° in front of the midline on either side).
source: We found that flies displayed anti-directional turning when presented with stimuli only in the front region or only just in front of the midline (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3b, c.

claim: Flies do not display anti-directional turning when moving stimuli are presented behind the midline.
source: They did not display anti-directional turning when moving stimuli were presented behind the midline (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3b, c.

claim: The anti-directional turning mechanism is different from behaviors that depend on posterior spatial location to elicit reverse turning.
source: This suggests a different mechanism from the behaviors that depend on posterior spatial location to elicit reverse turning (Tammero et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion comparing to prior work.

claim: In many trials, flies continue to turn opposite to the stimulus for several seconds.
source: Strikingly, in many trials, flies continued to turn opposite to the stimulus for several seconds, a behavior unlike brief saccades.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 3e data.

claim: When presented with high-contrast stimuli, flies maintain a negative turning index, indicating that sustained turns, and not high-velocity saccades, underlie anti-directional turning behavior.
source: When presented with high-contrast stimuli, flies maintained a negative turning index, indicating that sustained turns, and not high-velocity saccades, underlie this anti-directional turning behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 3f data.

claim: Anti-directional turning behavior is distinct from reports of anti-directional saccades.
source: As such, it appears distinct from the reports of anti-directional saccades.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the turning index analysis.

claim: T4 and T5 are required for directional neural responses.
source: Previous work demonstrated that T4 and T5 are required for directional neural responses (Schnell et al., 2012), as well as for optomotor turning (Maisak et al., 2013; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2018), for walking speed regulation (Creamer et al., 2018), and for responses to visual looming stimuli (Schilling and Borst, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: T4 and T5 are required for optomotor turning.
source: Previous work demonstrated that T4 and T5 are required for directional neural responses (Schnell et al., 2012), as well as for optomotor turning (Maisak et al., 2013; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2018), for walking speed regulation (Creamer et al., 2018), and for responses to visual looming stimuli (Schilling and Borst, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: T4 and T5 are required for walking speed regulation.
source: Previous work demonstrated that T4 and T5 are required for directional neural responses (Schnell et al., 2012), as well as for optomotor turning (Maisak et al., 2013; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2018), for walking speed regulation (Creamer et al., 2018), and for responses to visual looming stimuli (Schilling and Borst, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: T4 and T5 are required for responses to visual looming stimuli.
source: Previous work demonstrated that T4 and T5 are required for directional neural responses (Schnell et al., 2012), as well as for optomotor turning (Maisak et al., 2013; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2018), for walking speed regulation (Creamer et al., 2018), and for responses to visual looming stimuli (Schilling and Borst, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Flies in which T4 and T5 have been silenced display only minimal responses to motion stimuli, with anti-directional turning suppressed along with classical syn-directional turning.
source: Flies in which T4 and T5 had been silenced displayed only minimal responses to motion stimuli, with anti-directional turning suppressed along with classical syn-directional turning.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 4a data.

claim: Anti-directional behavior depends critically on signals from T4 and T5.
source: Thus, we conclude that, like optomotor turning behaviors, this anti-directional behavior depends critically on signals from T4 and T5.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the T4/T5 silencing experiments.

claim: HS cells integrate information from front-to-back and back-to-front selective T4 and T5 cells across the fly's visual field.
source: However, horizontal system (HS) cells are well-studied postsynaptic partners of T4 and T5 (Joesch et al., 2008; Joesch et al., 2010). These LPTCs integrate information from front-to-back and back-to-front selective T4 and T5 cells across the fly's visual field (Mauss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: HS cells have been implicated in visually evoked head turns.
source: HS cells have been implicated in visually evoked head turns (Kim et al., 2017) and body rotations in flight (Haikala et al., 2013) and in maintenance of direction during walking (Fujiwara et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: HS cells have been implicated in body rotations in flight.
source: HS cells have been implicated in visually evoked head turns (Kim et al., 2017) and body rotations in flight (Haikala et al., 2013) and in maintenance of direction during walking (Fujiwara et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: HS cells have been implicated in maintenance of direction during walking.
source: HS cells have been implicated in visually evoked head turns (Kim et al., 2017) and body rotations in flight (Haikala et al., 2013) and in maintenance of direction during walking (Fujiwara et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Silencing HS neurons results in small deficits in syn-directional turning behavior.
source: When we silenced HS neurons, we found small deficits in syn-directional turning behavior, consistent with prior results, but no deficits in anti-directional turning (Figure 4b), indicating that HS cells synaptic output is not required specifically for anti-directional turning behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Silencing HS neurons results in no deficits in anti-directional turning.
source: When we silenced HS neurons, we found small deficits in syn-directional turning behavior, consistent with prior results, but no deficits in anti-directional turning (Figure 4b), indicating that HS cells synaptic output is not required specifically for anti-directional turning behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: HS cell synaptic output is not required specifically for anti-directional turning behavior.
source: When we silenced HS neurons, we found small deficits in syn-directional turning behavior, consistent with prior results, but no deficits in anti-directional turning (Figure 4b), indicating that HS cells synaptic output is not required specifically for anti-directional turning behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the HS silencing experiments.

claim: CH LPTCs are GABAergic.
source: These cells are GABAergic and are both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic in the lobula plate (Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: CH LPTCs are both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic in the lobula plate.
source: These cells are GABAergic and are both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic in the lobula plate (Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: In blowflies, CH neurons play an inhibitory role in an interconnected LPTC circuit that shapes behavior.
source: In blowflies, these neurons play an inhibitory role in an interconnected LPTC circuit that shapes behavior (Borst and Weber, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Silencing CH neurons causes a small increase in syn-directional turning.
source: When we silenced CH neurons, we found a small increase in syn-directional turning and a decrease in anti-directional turning (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Silencing CH neurons causes a decrease in anti-directional turning.
source: When we silenced CH neurons, we found a small increase in syn-directional turning and a decrease in anti-directional turning (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Silencing CH neurons causes flies to turn more in the direction of motion.
source: Overall, silencing this neuron type caused the flies to turn more in the direction of motion.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the CH silencing results.

claim: CH activity contributes to the anti-directional turning response.
source: This result suggests that CH activity contributes to the anti-directional turning response.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the CH silencing experiments.

claim: Neurons beyond HS and CH neurons are likely involved in anti-directional turning, since adapting to back-to-front translational stimuli significantly affects the dynamics.
source: However, since adapting to back-to-front translational stimuli significantly affected the dynamics of anti-directional turning, it seems likely that other neurons beyond HS and CH neurons are involved, since these two neurons both respond selectively to front-to-back motion (Eckert and Dvorak, 1983; Joesch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the adaptation experiments and known properties of HS and CH neurons.

claim: HS and CH neurons both respond selectively to front-to-back motion.
source: However, since adapting to back-to-front translational stimuli significantly affected the dynamics of anti-directional turning, it seems likely that other neurons beyond HS and CH neurons are involved, since these two neurons both respond selectively to front-to-back motion (Eckert and Dvorak, 1983; Joesch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: T4 cells respond to drifting sinusoidal gratings in their preferred direction with increased calcium activity.
source: T4 cells, marked in orange (left), responded to drifting sinusoidal gratings with increased calcium activity (middle).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: T4 cell calcium activity increases with stimulus contrast.
source: When integrated across the stimulus presentation (right), calcium activity increased with stimulus contrast.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 5b and shown in the figure.

claim: T5 cell calcium activity increases with stimulus contrast.
source: As we increased the contrast of the preferred direction stimuli, we found that both T4 and T5 cells had increased calcium activity throughout the contrast range (Figure 5b, c, right), consistent with prior measurements (Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The responses of T4 and T5 cells do not capture the transition from syn-directional to anti-directional turning behavior.
source: Thus, the responses of T4 and T5 cells do not capture the transition from syn-directional to anti-directional turning behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the T4/T5 imaging data.

claim: Calcium signals in HS cells increase at the start of preferred direction stimuli presentation and stay high until the end of the presentation.
source: Calcium activity in HS cells followed similar trends to T4 and T5. Calcium signals increased at the start of preferred direction stimuli presentation and stayed high until the end of the presentation (Figure 5d, middle).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Increasing contrast causes stronger calcium responses in HS cells with a mild saturation effect at high contrast.
source: Increasing contrast caused stronger calcium responses with a mild saturation effect at high contrast (Figure 5d, right), consistent with prior voltage measurements (Joesch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The changes in the time course of optomotor behavior at high contrast are not related to changes in HS neuron activity.
source: These results indicate that the changes in the time course of optomotor behavior at high contrast are not related to changes in HS neuron activity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the HS imaging data.

claim: CH cells respond to visual stimuli more quickly than HS cells.
source: Finally, we measured calcium activity in CH cells. CH cells responded to visual stimuli more quickly than HS cells (Figure 5e, middle), and showed decreased calcium signals in response to null direction stimuli (Figure 5e, right).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5e.

claim: CH cells show decreased calcium signals in response to null direction stimuli.
source: Finally, we measured calcium activity in CH cells. CH cells responded to visual stimuli more quickly than HS cells (Figure 5e, middle), and showed decreased calcium signals in response to null direction stimuli (Figure 5e, right).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5e.

claim: CH cells show sustained responses to high-contrast stimuli.
source: However, they also showed sustained responses to high-contrast stimuli, as in T4, T5, and HS neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 5e data.

claim: The switch from syn- to anti-directional turning behavior is driven by cells downstream of or parallel to T4, T5, HS, and CH neurons.
source: These measurements suggest that the switch from syn- to anti-directional turning behavior is driven by cells downstream of or parallel to T4, T5, HS, and CH neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the imaging experiments.

claim: As flies age from 0.5 to 4 days post eclosion, the initial syn-directional turning becomes less transient and more sustained, indicative of a weaker anti-directional turning drive.
source: Strikingly, as flies aged from 0.5 to 4 days post eclosion (dpe), the initial syn-directional turning became less transient and more sustained, indicative of a weaker anti-directional turning drive.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 6 data.

claim: Dark-reared flies exhibit a stronger deceleration away from syn-directional turning, similar to that found in more juvenile flies.
source: Dark-reared flies exhibited a stronger deceleration away from syn-directional turning, similar to that found in more juvenile flies, arguing that visual input may sculpt the balance of syn- and anti-directional turning.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 6 data.

claim: Visual input may sculpt the balance of syn- and anti-directional turning.
source: Dark-reared flies exhibited a stronger deceleration away from syn-directional turning, similar to that found in more juvenile flies, arguing that visual input may sculpt the balance of syn- and anti-directional turning.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the dark-rearing experiments.

claim: In D. yakuba, anti-directional responses are stable across the first 4 days of adulthood.
source: Finally, we examined whether optomotor response plasticity could be detected in D. yakuba. However, in this species, anti-directional responses were stable across the first 4 days of adulthood, arguing that the role of visual experience in shaping these responses is itself evolutionarily tuned in drosophilids (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The role of visual experience in shaping optomotor responses is evolutionarily tuned in drosophilids.
source: Finally, we examined whether optomotor response plasticity could be detected in D. yakuba. However, in this species, anti-directional responses were stable across the first 4 days of adulthood, arguing that the role of visual experience in shaping these responses is itself evolutionarily tuned in drosophilids (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing D. melanogaster and D. yakuba developmental plasticity.

claim: The anti-directional turning behavior characterized in this study is distinct from previous reports of flies turning in the direction opposite to stimulus motion.
source: The anti-directional turning behavior we have characterized is distinct from previous reports of flies turning in the direction opposite to the stimulus motion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: Aliasing cannot explain the anti-directional turning results because the stimulus that maximally activates anti-directional behavior has a spatial frequency well below the Nyquist frequency of the fly eye.
source: Aliasing cannot explain our results because the stimulus that maximally activates anti-directional behavior has a spatial frequency of 1/60 cycles per degree, well below the Nyquist frequency of the fly eye (~1/10 cycles per degree) (Götz, 1970; Buchner, 1976) and below reports of higher acuity vision in flies (Juusola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an argument with citations to prior work.

claim: The Nyquist frequency of the fly eye is approximately 1/10 cycles per degree.
source: Aliasing cannot explain our results because the stimulus that maximally activates anti-directional behavior has a spatial frequency of 1/60 cycles per degree, well below the Nyquist frequency of the fly eye (~1/10 cycles per degree) (Götz, 1970; Buchner, 1976) and below reports of higher acuity vision in flies (Juusola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The anti-directional turning behavior is distinct from previously observed stimulus-density-dependent behavioral reversals.
source: Fourth, the behavior observed here also appears to be distinct from previously observed stimulus-density-dependent behavioral reversals (Katsov and Clandinin, 2008). Those previously reported behaviors showed immediate reversals, but it took ~1–2 s for flies in our paradigm to switch between optomotor and anti-directional behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to prior work with citation.

claim: The anti-directional turning observed is unlikely to be due to adaptation to contrast alone.
source: In mammalian retina, the direction preference of cells can switch because of upstream circuit adaptation (Rivlin-Etzion et al., 2012; Vlasits et al., 2014). However, we do not believe the anti-directional turning we observe has similar causes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with citations to prior work.

claim: The phenomenology of anti-directional turning argues that contrast adaptation is incomplete or heterogeneous among neurons.
source: Importantly, the phenomenology of the anti-directional turning also argues that the contrast adaptation is incomplete or heterogeneous among neurons, since contrast 1 and contrast 0.25 stimuli result in such different behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: Display brightness is a major cause of differences between this study's observations and prior studies that measured sustained optomotor turning in response to high-contrast stimuli.
source: Two major causes of this difference are likely display brightness and rearing conditions. Some experiments employ displays with mean luminances less than 5 cd/m2 (Rister et al., 2007; Seelig et al., 2010; Strother et al., 2017). Our screens, with a mean luminance of 100 cd/m2, are substantially brighter, but not especially bright when compared to natural scenes.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with citations to prior work.

claim: Rearing conditions are a major cause of differences between this study's observations and prior studies that measured sustained optomotor turning in response to high-contrast stimuli.
source: Two major causes of this difference are likely display brightness and rearing conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation.

claim: In daytime natural scenes, foliage and the ground have average luminances of 200–500 cd/m2.
source: In daytime natural scenes, foliage and the ground have average luminances of 200–500 cd/m2 and the sky has an average luminance of around 4000 cd/m2 (Frazor and Geisler, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: In daytime natural scenes, the sky has an average luminance of around 4000 cd/m2.
source: In daytime natural scenes, foliage and the ground have average luminances of 200–500 cd/m2 and the sky has an average luminance of around 4000 cd/m2 (Frazor and Geisler, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Temperature has known developmental effects on neural connectivity.
source: Temperature has known developmental effects on neural connectivity (Kiral et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The temporal tuning of anti-directional behavior (0.5–4 Hz) matches the tuning of T4, T5, and HS neurons as measured via calcium imaging or electrophysiology.
source: Optomotor behavior is tuned to visual stimuli in the range of 8–22 Hz (Tammero et al., 2004; Tuthill et al., 2013; Creamer et al., 2018; Strother et al., 2018), while anti-directional behavior is tuned to stimuli in the range of 0.5–4 Hz (Figure 2). Intriguingly, this slower tuning matches the tuning of T4, T5, and HS neurons, as measured via calcium imaging or electrophysiology (Joesch et al., 2008; Chiappe et al., 2010; Maisak et al., 2013; Creamer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that the difference in tuning between behavior and imaging are due to octopamine that is released during behavior but not necessarily during imaging.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the difference in tuning between behavior and imaging are due to octopamine that is released during behavior but not necessarily released during imaging (Chiappe et al., 2010; Arenz et al., 2017; Strother et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: T4 and T5 are required for behaviors with very different temporal tuning.
source: In this work, we demonstrate a motion-related behavior tuned to low frequencies, comparable to those in neural measurements, during behavior that requires T4 and T5 neurons. Overall, this suggests that T4 and T5 are required for behaviors with very different temporal tuning, which in turn suggests that the temporal tuning of behavior is not determined solely by T4 and T5 tuning, but by other, parallel pathways as well.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The temporal tuning of behavior is not determined solely by T4 and T5 tuning, but by other, parallel pathways as well.
source: In this work, we demonstrate a motion-related behavior tuned to low frequencies, comparable to those in neural measurements, during behavior that requires T4 and T5 neurons. Overall, this suggests that T4 and T5 are required for behaviors with very different temporal tuning, which in turn suggests that the temporal tuning of behavior is not determined solely by T4 and T5 tuning, but by other, parallel pathways as well.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The existence of turning in the direction opposite the stimulus motion requires a circuit that opposes the syn-directional optomotor turning response.
source: However, the existence of turning in the direction opposite the stimulus motion in D. melanogaster and in D. yakuba requires a different explanation. These experiments reveal that over long timescales, a circuit that opposes the syn-directional optomotor turning response can dominate the behavioral response.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The circuit that opposes syn-directional optomotor turning is not simply scaling the magnitude of turning responses, but must be implementing an antagonistic, subtractive operation.
source: Thus, this circuit is not simply scaling the magnitude of turning responses, but rather must be implementing an antagonistic, subtractive operation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The time constant of the autocorrelation of fly turning in free walking behavior is around 100 ms.
source: Measurements of free walking behavior have shown that the time constant of the autocorrelation of fly turning is around 100 ms (Katsov et al., 2017; DeAngelis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Opposing syn- and anti-directional turning circuits could be used to balance and tune the strength of turning responses on short timescales.
source: Opposing syn- and anti-directional turning circuits could be used to balance and tune the strength of turning responses on short timescales, while the anti-directional turning is revealed on longer timescales.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about circuit function.

claim: Subtractive processing predominates in computing motion signals in the visual systems of insects.
source: This sort of subtractive processing predominates in computing motion signals in the visual systems of insects (Mauss et al., 2015) and mammals (Rust et al., 2006), and could also explain the existence of syn- and anti-directional turning behaviors.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Subtractive processing predominates in computing motion signals in the visual systems of mammals.
source: This sort of subtractive processing predominates in computing motion signals in the visual systems of insects (Mauss et al., 2015) and mammals (Rust et al., 2006), and could also explain the existence of syn- and anti-directional turning behaviors.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Turning in response to rotational stimuli is likely driven by circuits with opposing influences on turning direction.
source: This behavior suggests that turning in response to rotational stimuli is not a simple reflex. Instead, the turning is likely driven by circuits with opposing influences on turning direction.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the overall findings.

claim: The circuits driving turning appear to differentially adapt to the direction and contrast of the stimulus.
source: These circuits appear to differentially adapt to the direction and contrast of the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the adaptation experiments.
